sections.h2: What does the Colorado homestead exemption protect?
sections.html:
The Colorado homestead exemption shields part of the equity in your home from creditors who hold a court judgment. It is separate from the property tax breaks for seniors, and the two get mixed up often.

Under C.R.S. 38-41-201, a homestead is exempt from execution and attachment for debts, contracts and civil obligations, up to a set amount of actual cash value above any liens in place when a levy happens. The protected amounts are:

Who occupies the homeProtected amount
An owner or the owner's family$250,000
An owner, spouse or dependent who is elderly or disabled$350,000

The statute defines elderly as age sixty or older. Disabled means a physical or mental impairment that substantially keeps the person from useful work in any job that exists in the community and fits their competence. The text we read is the 2024 edition as published by the Colorado legislature and mirrored on a public statute site, so confirm the figures against the current edition before you rely on them.

sections.h2: Do I have to file anything to claim it?
sections.html:
Usually no. Section 38-41-202 says the exemption is deemed created and can be claimed when the home is occupied and the property is the right kind of homestead.

There is a catch for debts older than a certain date. The statute says the exemption cannot be claimed against an obligation incurred before July 1, 1975, unless the owner recorded a written homestead statement with the county clerk and recorder. That date makes it a niche rule today.

A recorded statement still matters in one way. When an owner or spouse records the instrument, both spouses must sign to convey or encumber the property. Without a recording, a homestead that arises automatically can be conveyed or encumbered by the owner alone, with no other signature needed.

For a seller, that gives a clear checklist:

  • Search the county records for a recorded homestead declaration.
  • If one exists, plan for both spouses to sign the deed.
  • If none exists, only the owner of record needs to sign.

sections.h2: Does the home have to be lived in?
sections.html:
Yes. Section 38-41-203 says the property is exempt only while it is occupied as a home by the owner or the owner's family.

That rule affects houses people are about to sell. A house that has sat empty after a move, or one that is rented out, may no longer qualify for the protection. If a judgment creditor is in the picture, the date you moved out can matter.

The statute does not use the words vacant or rental, so a lawyer should read the facts before anyone relies on the exemption. For tenant-occupied properties, the eviction and landlord rules are the better starting point.

sections.h2: What happens when a creditor tries to force a sale of a homestead?
sections.html:
A creditor has to clear several hurdles first. Under C.R.S. 38-41-206, the creditor must file an affidavit with the county clerk and recorder and with the sheriff or other officer who would levy.

  • A description of the homestead and the name of the claimant.
  • The fair market value of the property.
  • A statement that value minus prior liens is above the exemption amount the claimant qualifies for.
  • A statement that no earlier execution from the same judgment has been levied.
  • A second affidavit from a professionally qualified independent appraiser with the same value information.

If the winning bid at the sale does not exceed seventy percent of the appraiser's fair market value, the proceedings end. The officer records a release of all levies, the person who started the case pays the costs, and the owner's title is not harmed.

If a sale does go through, the money is paid out in a fixed order:

  1. Prior liens and encumbrances.
  2. The homestead claimant, up to the exemption amount.
  3. Costs and expenses of the sale.
  4. The judgment.
  5. Anything left over, back to the claimant.

A judgment creditor who is the winning bidder must pay cash for the exemption plus costs, and cannot apply the exempt amount against the judgment.

sections.h2: Are the sale proceeds protected if I sell the house?
sections.html:
For a limited time, yes. C.R.S. 38-41-207 exempts the proceeds from execution or attachment for three years after you receive them, provided you keep the money separate so it can always be identified.

That covers the exempt amount when the owner sells the property, proceeds of a sale under section 38-41-206, and insurance money for destroyed homestead property held to restore or replace it.

There is also a carryover. If you use the proceeds to buy another home, the same exemption you had on the old house applies to the new one. It does not work against a vendor's lien or the holder of a purchase money mortgage on the new property.

The practical tip is simple. If you are selling a house while a creditor is pressing, do not mix the sale check into a general account. A separate account keeps the money traceable, which is what the statute asks for.

sections.h2: How is this different from the senior property tax exemption?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption is a creditor shield. The senior property tax exemption lowers a tax bill. They sit in different parts of the law and are run by different offices.

The Division of Property Taxation describes the senior exemption on its program notice and says each county accepts applications on a yearly cycle, with the application window opening January 1. County assessors take the applications.

The age, ownership and occupancy tests and the exempt share of value are set out in the state program summary higher on this page. Ask your county assessor for the current year's form.

If you plan to sell during the year, ask the county assessor how a sale affects an application already filed.

sections.h2: How do property taxes get paid when a Colorado house is sold?
sections.html:
Colorado lets the taxpayer pay the bill in full or in two installments, and section 39-10-104.5 sets the schedule. Any split between buyer and seller is a term of the sale contract.

OptionDue date
Pay in fullOn or before April 30, with no interest through that date
First halfLast day of February
Second halfJune 15

Interest runs at one percent per month once a payment is late. The statute says no installments are allowed on a total under $25, which must be paid in full by April 30. You can read the rule on the statute page.

Confirm the balance and any delinquent interest with the county treasurer before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: What does the county charge to record the deed?
sections.html:
Besides ordinary recording fees, a deed filed with the county clerk and recorder carries a documentary fee. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102 it is one cent for each $100 of consideration, and no fee applies when the consideration is $500 or less.

The person who offers the deed for recording pays it. For a $400,000 sale that works out to $40, using the one-cent rate as written in the statute.

If you are selling a house with a judgment or lien attached, we are glad to walk through the numbers with you, and we suggest a Colorado attorney for the legal questions.

faqs.q: How much does the Colorado homestead exemption protect?
faqs.a: $250,000 for a home occupied by an owner or the owner's family, and $350,000 when the occupant is an elderly or disabled owner, spouse or dependent. Elderly means sixty or older under the statute.

faqs.q: Do I need to record a homestead declaration?
faqs.a: No. The exemption arises automatically if the occupancy and property-type rules are met. Recording a statement is only needed for older debts and changes who must sign a deed.

faqs.q: Does the homestead exemption stop me from selling my house?
faqs.a: No. It limits what a judgment creditor can collect from the home. It does not block a voluntary sale. A recorded declaration means both spouses must sign the deed.

faqs.q: How long are the sale proceeds protected?
faqs.a: Three years after you receive them, if you keep them separate and identifiable. If you buy another home with the money, the same exemption carries over to it.

faqs.q: Can a creditor force the sale of my home for any price?
faqs.a: No. If the winning bid is seventy percent or less of the appraised fair market value in the creditor's appraiser affidavit, the proceedings end and the creditor pays the costs.

faqs.q: When are Colorado property taxes due?
faqs.a: In full by April 30, or in two halves, the last day of February and June 15. Interest runs at one percent per month on late payments.

faqs.q: What is the documentary fee on a Colorado deed?
faqs.a: One cent for each $100 of consideration, collected by the county clerk and recorder, with no fee when the consideration is $500 or less.
